title: My Heart Is Steadfast, O God
superscription: A song. A Psalm of David.

verses.text: My heart is steadfast, O God; I will sing and make music with all my being.
Awake, O harp and lyre! I will awaken the dawn.
I will praise You, O LORD, among the nations; I will sing Your praises among the peoples.
For Your loving devotion extends beyond the heavens, and Your faithfulness reaches to the clouds.
Be exalted, O God, above the heavens; may Your glory cover all the earth.
Respond and save us with Your right hand, that Your beloved may be delivered.
God has spoken from His sanctuary: "I will triumph! I will parcel out Shechem and apportion the Valley of Succoth.
Gilead is Mine, and Manasseh is Mine; Ephraim is My helmet, Judah is My scepter.
Moab is My washbasin; upon Edom I toss My sandal; over Philistia I shout in triumph."
Who will bring me to the fortified city? Who will lead me to Edom?
Have You not rejected us, O God? Will You no longer march out, O God, with our armies?
Give us aid against the enemy, for the help of man is worthless.
With God we will perform with valor, and He will trample our enemies.

context.author: The title says “A song. A Psalm of David.” It joins the end of Psalm 57 (57:7-11) and the end of Psalm 60 (60:5-12), turning a lament and a defeat into a song of confidence.
context.genre: Psalm: a song or prayer in Hebrew poetry
context.audience: Israel at worship, and the nations called to join
context.setting: “My heart is steadfast, O God; I will sing and make music with all my being. Awake, O harp and lyre! I will awaken the dawn” (vv.1-2). “For Your loving devotion extends beyond the heavens” (v.4). “Be exalted, O God, above the heavens; may Your glory cover all the earth” (v.5). Then God speaks from His sanctuary, claiming the whole land as His: “I will parcel out Shechem and apportion the Valley of Succoth. Gilead is Mine, and Manasseh is Mine; Ephraim is My helmet, Judah is My scepter” (vv.7-8). Israel’s enemies are His servants: “Moab is My washbasin; upon Edom I toss My sandal” (v.9). The king asks, “Who will lead me to Edom?” (v.10), and ends, “Give us aid against the enemy, for the help of man is worthless. With God we will perform with valor” (vv.12-13).
context.custom: Reusing older psalms in new settings was common in Israel’s worship; Psalm 70 repeats Psalm 40:13-17 in the same way. A washbasin was for washing a servant’s or guest’s feet, and tossing a sandal over land was a gesture of claiming it (Ruth 4:7). Shechem lay west of the Jordan and Succoth east of it, so God claims both sides of the river.
context.timelineImmediate: Psalm 109 is a fierce prayer against false accusers.
context.timelineBible: Paul wrote, “If God is for us, who can be against us?” (Romans 8:31). Jesus taught that apart from Him “you can do nothing” (John 15:5), like v.12.

translation.meaning: Edom, “red,” the land of Esau’s descendants.

gospelParallels.note: Apart from Me you can do nothing.

overview.summary: David’s steadfast heart wakes the dawn with praise, and he trusts God’s promise to claim the land and defeat Edom, because the help of man is worthless but with God there is victory.
overview.settingLine: Two old songs made into one battle hymn.

history.t: David’s victory in the Valley of Salt.

archaeology.t: The remains of Shechem with its great Middle Bronze Age temple and gate.
Probably Succoth, in the Jordan Valley, where the Balaam inscription was found.

overview.discussion: The psalm reuses older prayers for a new moment. Is there a psalm I have prayed before that God is giving me again for something new?
overview.book: The book of Psalms · 150 psalms (all 150 in the app). Israel’s songs and prayers: praise, lament, thanks, trust and wisdom, many of them by David.
overview.author: David

timeline.label: With God we will do valiantly
